newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul mayor seeks to run in presidential election.
newsitem.headline: Seoul mayor seeks to run in presidential election.

text.p: The independent-minded mayor of Seoul has decided to run in South Korea's presidential vote, a move political analysts said could split the ruling party.
Cho Soon sent his aide to the opposition Democratic Party on Monday to accept an invitation to seek party nomination for the presidential race, a party statement said.
Cho's aide, Kim Sang-nam, told Reuters that Cho would step down as mayor within a month to run in the December 18 election. Cho was not available for comment.
"The mayor is seeking the presidency to bring an end to old politics and help Korea overcome its current problems," said Kim, a member of Seoul City Council.
Cho, a widely respected economist, in 1995 became South Korea's first elected mayor of Seoul, home for about a quarter of the country's 44 million population.

The Democratic Party, with 11 of 299 seats in parliament, is the smallest among the three opposition parties and no analyst said he had any chance of emerging as the successor of President Kim Young-sam, who is barred from seeking re-election.

The ruling New Korea Party's candidate, former supreme court judge Lee Hoi-chang, had been widely expected to win the poll but political analysts said Cho's decision could make the outcome unpredictable.
They said Cho, like Lee, was a political novice and not tainted by a corrupt political system hit by a string of bribes-for-kickbacks scandals.

"Cho could eat into a support base formerly regarded as Lee's. This could stoke challenges within the ruling party, particularly among factions opposing his candidacy," said Lee Ki-tak, who lectures in politics at Seoul's Yonsei University.
"Cho's candidacy could cause some New Korea Party presidential aspirants to leave the party and run as independents, resulting in the party's break-up," he said.
Analysts have said the most difficult task Lee Hoi-chang faced was to hold the ruling camp together after last month's openly divisive battle to win party nomination.

"Lee Hoi-chang's critics within the ruling party could argue that he is not a strong enough candidate and declare themselves as independent candidates," said Kim Kwang-woong, a political science professor at Seoul National University.
"This could spawn candidates, which will make the presidential vote chaotic," he said.
Lee Hoi-chang's popularity had already been waning because of a scandal surrounding his two sons' exemption from mandatory 30-month military service.
Lee has denied opposition accusations that his sons intentionally lost weight to avoid military service.

"As long as the ruling party keeps its support behind one candidate, Cho's running will damage the opposition whose ticket will be split into three," said Korea University political science professor Choi Jang-jip.

The main opposition National Congress for New Politics and the smaller United Liberal Democrats have nominated their leaders Kim Dae-jung and Kim Jong-pil respectively as their torchbearers in December.
Choi said the ruling party, which has a better-oiled political machine, has always won past presidential votes.
"But if the New Korea Party is divided, it is a totally new ball game," he said.
